catalog_quote: ARDEN 1910 para. 29 (pp. 17-18, page image): "When a Tamil word has both long and short vowels, a certain amount of emphasis naturally falls upon the long, as in the word குமாரன் [kumāraṉ] a son. But when all the vowels in a word are short, or all long, the emphasis is always thrown upon the first syllable. In many English words the emphasis is thrown upon the second syllable, as in the words support, refresh, corrupt. Great care must be taken not to do this in Tamil; but the emphasis must always be thrown upon the first syllable; as மரம் [maram] a tree, அனுப்பு [aṉuppu] send (thou). Compare the pronunciation of the Tamil word அவர் [avar] he with the English word aver." Para. 81 (p. 30): "This initial உ or இ is pronounced very slightly, and no emphasis is made upon it. sweep_summary: Two Glottolog title hits for Tamil, neither read and neither likely about word stress. Pittman 1971 ('Tense vs. lax word-base prosodies.. Tamil retroflexion vs. Hindi aspiration') is a Firthian/SIL feature-domain paper in Vol. I of the 1968 Madras Tamil Studies proceedings; only Vol. 2 is open (archive.org tdl.22993), and its preface, contents and printed pp. 249-253 were read from saved page images to confirm the paper is not there; Google Books gives the opening sentence only (no page view). Thananjayarajasingham 1974 ('Adjectival system in Jaffna Tamil: a prosodic analysis', Indian Linguistics 35: 31-43) is Firthian prosodic analysis of adjective morphology in the Sri Lankan dialect, print only, no open copy anywhere found. Both marked unclear/low priority; no new first-hand stress statement was read in this search of works with stress in the title, so the catalog's Arden 1910 deciding source (already flagged at-risk by the prior check on Andronov 1989 and Keane 2003/2007) stands unchanged by these two titles. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books API, HathiTrust, fatcat and scholar.archive.org metadata, Crossref, and the Google Books GData feed. and.

audit.recode_to: conflict ('descriptions disagree'), leaning hedged weak initial prominence if the catalog privileges instrumental over impressionistic sources: impressionistic descriptions split between a vowel-length/quantity-conditioned movable stress (Arden 1910 para. 29; Andronov 1989 sec. 10 'weak, movable, free.. place not fixed.. long vowel generally stressed', with speaker variation) and fixed initial stress (Keane 2003: 'most descriptions favour either fixed initial stress or a quantity-sensitive dynamic system'), while every instrumental study held (Keane 2003, 2006 abstract, 2007) finds weak, non-lexical, weight-blind word-INITIAL prominence (Keane 2007: L turning-point inside the initial syllable in 465 of 467 phrase-medial tokens in a design that systematically varied syllable quantity, incl. light-heavy words). Do not keep weight class CVV as the classification of record unless Christdas 1988 or Keane 2006 full text states a length condition that survives the instrumental evidence.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: Arden 1910 paras 29 and 81 are verbatim on the held archive.org page images (pp. 17-18, 30) and djvu scanned; Keane 2004, Keane 2006 abstract and Schiffman 1999 passages are in the copies we hold at the stated lines. (2) The deciding source is a 1910 missionary teaching grammar; the weight condition (CVV heavy) and the initial default both come only from it. For a language with 163 Glottolog descriptive refs, including a 482-pp phonology dissertation (Christdas 1988), two reference grammars (Andronov 2004, Asher 1989) and an instrumental JIPA study of exactly this question (Keane 2006), that is not the best available basis. sources.quote: 'The stress in Modern Tamil is weak, movable, free, quantitative-dynamic-tonic. ... The place of the stressed syllable in word is not fixed; e.g., veyil ["veyil], peyar ["peyAr] ... tamizh [tA"mIzh], viral [vI"rAl], nizhal [nI"zhAl] ... kizhavi [kIzhA"vi] ... In words which have geminated consonants or consonant clusters the stressed vowel frequently precedes the consonant group ... But this is not always the rule ...
